PMGT1711 Week 10

PMGT1711 Week 10 - Leverage Points, Paradigms and Risk Interdependencies

Leverage and Learning

A leverage point is a place to intervene in a system where a relatively small change may produce a substantial change in behaviour or outcomes. Leverage concerns the mechanism through which an intervention works, not simply its visibility or cost. A deep intervention may face resistance or take time to affect outcomes; depth does not guarantee that it is always the most appropriate choice.

Learning can occur at different levels:

Learning loop

Focus

Guiding idea

Single-loop

Correct errors within existing assumptions and procedures

Do things right

Double-loop

Examine causes and reconsider the approach or framing

Do the right things

Triple-loop

Question values and how the system decides what is right

Examine why the system, processes and desired outcomes exist

Single-loop correction can be useful without changing the wider purpose. Double-loop learning reframes the approach. Triple-loop learning examines the values and decision processes underlying the framing itself.

System Concepts

Concept

Meaning

Stock

An accumulated quantity or system state

Flow

A rate that increases or decreases a stock

Feedback

A chain of effects that returns to influence an earlier condition

Delay

A separation in time between an action and its effect or between information and response

Parameter

A numerical setting that affects operation

For a stock measured in units and flows measured in units per time period, the basic relationship is:

Change in stock = total inflow over the period - total outflow over the period

Thus the final stock equals the initial stock plus this change. Flow rates must be converted into quantities over the chosen interval before being added to a stock. A stock and a flow are not interchangeable quantities.

Balancing feedback, also called negative feedback, counteracts a change or a departure from a target. Reinforcing feedback, also called positive feedback, amplifies a change, whether growth or decline. Positive does not mean beneficial, and negative does not mean harmful.

Delays can make a response arrive after conditions have changed. Repeated correction before earlier effects become visible can produce excessive responses and oscillation.

Sustainability and Project Purpose

The triple bottom line considers People, Planet and Profit: social wellbeing, environmental consequences and economic viability. This broadens evaluation beyond the iron triangle of cost, time and scope.

Human sustainability includes safe conditions, reasonable working hours and good health. Efficient delivery against a narrow cost or schedule target does not establish that these wider outcomes are acceptable.

Paradigms

A paradigm is a shared set of beliefs, values, techniques and exemplary ways of solving problems. It shapes what a community regards as a meaningful problem and a legitimate answer. Thomas Kuhn used the concept to examine scientific change, including shifts in astronomical explanations associated with Ptolemy and Copernicus.

In projects, consider Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP), an integrated approach to managing business information and processes. Treating ERP as an information technology installation emphasises technical implementation. Treating it as business change also brings organisational processes, responsibilities and behaviour into scope. The technology can be similar while the understood purpose and necessary work differ.

Meadows' Twelve Leverage Points

The hierarchy runs from number 12, relatively shallow, toward number 1, relatively deep. The numbers are labels in the hierarchy, not measured quantities of effect.

A separate four-level depth scale runs in the opposite numerical direction:

• Depth 1: very shallow.

• Depth 2: shallow.

• Depth 3: deep.

• Depth 4: very deep.

These scales support interpretation rather than an automatic numerical calculation. Classification depends on the actual mechanism, and some interventions span categories.

12: Constants, Parameters and Numbers

Examples include tax rates, subsidy amounts, standards and numerical limits. Such changes are common because they are visible and comparatively easy to specify, but may leave the basic pattern of behaviour intact.

Interest-rate adjustments do not by themselves eliminate business cycles. Donation caps or an age threshold for alcohol sales illustrate numerical settings; identifying a number does not by itself prove a particular policy effect. Near a critical threshold, however, a small numerical change can sometimes trigger a large transition in system behaviour.

11: Buffers

A buffer is a stock that can absorb a disturbance relative to the flows affecting it. A larger lake may absorb a limited warm-water discharge with less temperature variation than a smaller volume, depending on discharge conditions. This does not imply that any lake can absorb unlimited heat or pollution.

Larger buffers can stabilise a system but can also reduce flexibility or impose costs. Physical capacity may be difficult to alter. Just-in-time inventory seeks to keep inventory closely aligned with immediate requirements; it contrasts with retaining a large reserve.

10: Material Stock-and-Flow Structure

Physical layout shapes what can move, where and at what rate. A road network concentrating traffic through Budapest illustrates how structure can generate congestion and pollution that signal timing alone cannot resolve. Diverting industrial wastewater to a treatment plant requires changes to physical pipes and connections.

Physical redesign can be powerful but expensive, especially after infrastructure is built.

9: Delays

The significance of a delay depends on how quickly the surrounding system changes. A treatment plant requiring five years to build and expected to operate for about thirty years creates a mismatch between current problems, construction response and uncertain future capacity.

Not all delays can be readily shortened. Some organisational delays can be changed, such as the interval between meetings needed for an important decision. A quicker response is useful only if it improves the relevant feedback rather than encouraging premature action.

8: Balancing Feedback Strength

A balancing process needs a target, a way to detect a departure and a response capable of correcting it. A thermostat exemplifies these elements.

A charge linked to measured wastewater concentration connects environmental measurement to a corrective incentive. A performance-management process may connect Key Performance Indicators (KPIs), measurable indicators of performance, to corrective staffing or management decisions.

The response must be strong enough relative to the disturbance. Monitoring without an effective response mechanism does not complete the corrective loop.

7: Reinforcing Feedback Gain

Gain is the degree to which a process amplifies change. Blood clotting includes chemical processes that activate more platelets, with balancing mechanisms limiting the response. Influenza transmission can create further exposure and hence additional transmission.

Reducing harmful amplification may be more effective than continually accelerating compensating responses. Uncontrolled reinforcement can overwhelm a system's corrective capacity.

6: Information Flows

Changing who receives information can change decisions without rebuilding material infrastructure. A visible household electricity meter, rather than an inaccessible one, illustrates how awareness of consumption can support a response. Self-monitoring of blood pressure or blood glucose similarly changes access to actionable information.

The relevant mechanism is newly available information and its connection to action. Merely distributing more information is not sufficient if nobody can interpret or use it.

5: Rules

Rules establish incentives, penalties, constraints and who can make decisions. Examples include chemical-discharge laws and pollution-related tax arrangements.

Changing only the numerical tax rate is a parameter intervention. Redesigning the incentive or compliance regime is a rule intervention. The classification follows what changes, not the presence of the word tax.

4: Self-Organisation

Self-organisation is the capacity to generate or modify structures, feedback, information flows and rules. It is broader than changing one isolated rule.

Microorganisms developing new ways to interact with pollutants illustrate adaptive capability. Biodegradation is biological breakdown of a substance. Bioaccumulation is its build-up within organisms; accumulation must not be equated with harmless elimination.

3: Goals

A goal defines the purpose toward which the system operates. Changing a lake's management purpose from unrestricted use toward tourism or conservation can reorganise monitoring, enforcement and access arrangements.

Goal changes can redirect parameters, information, feedback and adaptive activity. Efficient pursuit of an inappropriate goal is not sufficient for overall success.

2: Mindset or Paradigm

Paradigms support the selection of goals and the acceptability of structures and rules. Seeing nature mainly as a resource for human use differs from seeing it as an interconnected living system requiring care.

Making anomalies and failures visible to people willing to reconsider assumptions can contribute to change. A paradigm shift is not automatically easy, immediate or uncontested.

1: Transcending Paradigms

Transcending paradigms means recognising that every worldview has limits and being able to consider alternatives without rigid dependence on one framework. It is different from replacing one paradigm with another: the latter remains a change at number 2, whereas number 1 concerns one's relationship to paradigms themselves.

Four Broad Intervention Families

Family

Meadows numbers

Focus

Parameters

12-10

9-7

These families move broadly from shallow to deep. They are not interchangeable with the separate depth 1-4 ratings: the family boundaries do not reproduce every depth rating.

Parameters can also be described as material features, and feedbacks as processes. A causal account asks how mechanisms produce effects; a teleological account asks what purposes an activity serves. This contrast concerns explanation and purpose, not a required chronological order of action.

Diagnosing an Intervention

A useful diagnosis connects the challenge to its underlying mechanism:

Define the system and the observed problem.

Identify relevant complexity: dependencies, technical uncertainty, contested direction or relationships.

Establish what the proposed intervention changes: numbers, material structure, feedback, information, rules, adaptive capacity, goals or assumptions.

Explain the leverage category and depth judgement.

Identify participants, decision rights and likely resistance.

Consider costs, delays and unintended consequences.

Specify what feedback would indicate improvement.

Routine double-sided printing illustrates a shallow operational adjustment. Making it a mandatory default can also change rules; the classification depends on the intervention's design.

Sustainability interventions can target manager bonuses, team rewards, procurement criteria, professional education, management methods, safety requirements, environmental laws and the visibility of building ratings. These labels alone do not establish their leverage depth. For example, a reward may simply change an incentive amount or may be part of a redesigned decision system.

National Australian Built Environment Rating System (NABERS) and Green Star are building sustainability assessment and rating systems. Making such ratings visible can be analysed as an information-flow change when the mechanism is to inform consequential decisions.

System dynamics models stocks, flows, feedback and delays to examine changing behaviour over time. Using such a model can support feedback diagnosis, but the model itself does not guarantee that the organisation will act on what it reveals.

A disposable-cup problem similarly requires an explanation of what a proposed measure changes; the problem label alone cannot identify its leverage category.

Risk Interdependencies

Risks can interact rather than operate independently. The Risk Interdependencies tool examines relationships among already identified risks, especially harmful compounding processes. It complements conventional risk identification and may reveal additional risks during discussion.

It is suited to small and medium projects, can take approximately 20-60 minutes and should be repeated because relationships change.

Complexity dimension

Relevant risk connections

Structural

Numerous dependencies and risks emerging from their interaction

Technical

Design uncertainty combining with cost and time uncertainty

Directional

Conflicting interpretations, priorities or political agendas

Relational

Communication gaps, power imbalances, conflict and distrust reinforcing one another

Procedure

Bring together the project manager, project director and relevant specialists, such as finance, legal or environmental experts.

Begin with approximately twenty predefined risks.

Use small discussion groups of two or three people.

Give each risk an identifier and represent it on a prepared risk circle.

Construct an influence matrix using the same risk set for rows and columns.

Mark where one risk influences another.

Transfer important connections to a directed diagram, using different colours to preserve different groups' contributions if needed.

Combine the diagrams and examine dependencies and feedback loops.

A smaller matrix can demonstrate the technique; seven risks are not a required total.

Influence Matrix Direction

Influencing risks appear in columns. Influenced risks appear in rows. A mark at row C and column D therefore means that D influences C.

                              Influencing risk
                         C                     D
Influenced risk C        -                     X
Influenced risk D        blank                 -

X at row C, column D: D -> C
Blank: no influence entered in that cell
Dash on diagonal: self-entry not used in this illustration

The diagram arrow follows the same direction: influencing risk to influenced risk.

Negative Publicity and Sponsor Withdrawal

Let risk D represent negative media coverage generated by activists and risk C represent withdrawal of a major sponsor.

D: Negative media coverage -> C: Sponsor withdrawal

This relationship does not establish that sponsor withdrawal also causes the media coverage. Reverse influence requires its own justification.

A Three-Risk Cycle

A risk network can contain the following cycle, where numbers identify risks rather than probabilities or magnitudes:

[2] -> [18] -> [12] -> [2]

The cycle shows a closed chain of influence. Without the polarity of each relationship, it cannot automatically be classified as reinforcing or balancing.

Polarity describes whether a change in one variable tends to change the next in the same direction or the opposite direction, other conditions held equal. To classify a loop, examine every connection and the combined effect around the loop. A causal loop diagram explicitly represents such causal relationships, often including their polarities.

The management aim is to identify interventions that weaken harmful amplification or improve relevant information, rules and responses. Treating every risk as independent can miss the mechanism through which a moderate problem becomes a larger project failure.
